en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Saṅghādisesa Offenses
13. The Training Rule on Corrupters of Families At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, there were two monks named Assaji and Punabbasuka who resided at Kīṭāgiri; they were shameless and evil monks.
They practice such improper conduct as this:
they plant flower seedlings or have them planted; they water them or have them watered; they pluck flowers or have them plucked; they string them or have them strung;
they make single-stalk garlands or have them made; they make double-stalk garlands or have them made.

They themselves make *mañjarika* garlands or have them made; they themselves make *vidhūtika* garlands or have them made; they themselves make *vaṭaṁsaka* garlands or have them made; they themselves make *āveḷa* garlands or have them made; they themselves make breast-ornaments (*uracchada*) or have them made.
They themselves carry single-stalked garlands for noble women, noble daughters, noble maidens, noble daughters-in-law, and noble slave-girls, or have them carried;
they themselves carry double-stalked garlands or have them carried; they themselves carry *mañjarika* garlands...

They take away [ornaments], and they have them taken away; they take away the *vidhūtika* (head-ornament), and they have it taken away; they take away the *vaṭaṃsaka* (ear-ornament), and they have it taken away;
they take away the *āveḷa* (garland), and they have it taken away; they take away the breast-cover (*uracchada*), and they have it taken away.

They eat from the same vessel and drink from the same bowl together with women of good family, daughters of good family, young girls of good family, daughters-in-law of good family, and female slaves of good family.
They sit on a single seat; they lie down on a single bed; they lie down on a single covering; they lie down under a single cloak; they lie down under both a single covering and a single cloak;
they eat at improper times; they drink intoxicants; they wear garlands, perfumes, and ointments;
they dance, sing, play instruments, and perform on stage.
When she dances, they dance; when she dances, they sing; when she dances, they play instruments; when she dances, they perform rhythmic movements.
When she sings, they dance; when she sings, they sing; when she sings, they play instruments; when she sings, they perform rhythmic movements.
When she plays instruments, they dance; when she plays instruments, they sing; when she plays instruments, they play instruments; when she plays instruments, they perform rhythmic movements.
They dance to the accompaniment of lāsentī songs, they sing to the accompaniment of lāsentī songs, they play instruments to the accompaniment of lāsentī songs,
and they cause others to dance to the accompaniment of lāsentī songs; they play at eight-row chess, they play at ten-row chess, they play in the air,
they play on a path for circumambulation, they play with *santikā* pieces, they play with *khalikā* pieces, they play with *ghaṭikā* pieces, and they play with dice.
They play with dice, they play with a cloth-strip, they play with a crooked stick, they play with a top, they play with a spinning-top,
they play with a leaf-cup, they play with toy chariots, they play with bows, they play with syllables,
they play with mental exercises, and they play with whatever is available.
They train in elephant-riding, they train in horsemanship, they train in chariot-driving, they train in archery, and they train in swordsmanship;
they run before elephants, they run before horses, and they run forward and backward before chariots;
they shout, they clap their hands, they wrestle, and they fight with their fists.

Even in the midst of the stage, they spread out their outer robes (*saṅghāṭī*) and say to the dancers, “Dance here, sister,” and they even give them forehead marks; they engage in various kinds of improper conduct.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu who had completed the rains retreat in Kāsī was traveling toward Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One and arrived at Kīṭāgiri.
Then, in the morning, that bhikkhu dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kīṭāgiri for alms.
He was graceful in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching; with downcast eyes, he was perfected in deportment.
When people saw that bhikkhu, they said: “Who is this who looks so weak, so dull, so frowning?
Who will give almsfood to one who has approached us like this? But our masters, Assaji and Punabbasu—”
"Gentle, kindly, pleasant in speech, preceded by smiles, speakers of welcome and greetings, free from frowns, open-faced, and the first to speak—
alms should indeed be given to such as these.
Then a certain lay follower saw that bhikkhu walking for alms in Kīṭāgiri.
Having seen him, he approached that bhikkhu; having approached and paid homage to that bhikkhu, he said this: "Venerable sir, have you received alms?
"Friend, no alms have been received.
"Come, venerable sir, let us go to the house."
Then that lay follower, having led that bhikkhu to his home and fed him, said this:
"Venerable sir, where will the noble one go?
"Friend, I shall go to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One."
“In that case, venerable sir, pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, and say this:
‘Venerable sir, the residence at Kīṭāgiri is corrupt.
Those known as Assaji and Punabbasu, the residents of Kīṭāgiri, are shameless, evil monks.’”
They practice such improper conduct as this:
they plant flowering shrubs themselves or have them planted; they water them themselves or have them watered... [and so on] ...they practice various kinds of improper conduct.
Furthermore, Bhante, those people who were formerly faithful and confident have now become faithless and devoid of confidence.
“Those former sources of offerings for the Saṅgha have now been cut off.
Virtuous bhikkhus are being neglected, while wicked bhikkhus dwell there.
It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would send bhikkhus to Kīṭāgiri, so that this residence at Kīṭāgiri may be established.”
“Very well, friend,” that bhikkhu replied to the lay follower and set out for Sāvatthī.

Traveling by stages, he arrived at Sāvatthī, at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, where the Blessed One was staying. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to exchange greetings with visiting bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One said this to that bhikkhu:
“I hope you are bearing up, bhikkhu; I hope you are getting by;
I hope you have come along the road without too much fatigue?”
“And from where have you come, bhikkhu?
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is livable, Blessed One.
And I have come along the road, Bhante, without much fatigue.”
"Here, venerable sir, having spent the rains retreat among the Kāsīs, I was coming to Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One when I stayed at Kīṭāgiri.
Then, venerable sir, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I entered Kīṭāgiri for alms.
There, venerable sir, a certain lay follower saw me walking for alms in Kīṭāgiri."
Having seen me, he approached where I was; having approached and paid homage to me, he said this: “Venerable sir, has alms been obtained?
“Friend, no alms have been obtained.
“Come, venerable sir, let us go to the house.”
Then, venerable sir, that lay follower led me to his home, fed me, and said this:
“Where, venerable sir, will the noble one go?
“I shall go to Sāvatthī, friend, to see the Blessed One.”
"In that case, venerable sir, pay homage with your head at the Blessed One’s feet in my name, and say this:
‘Venerable sir, the dwelling at Kīṭāgiri is corrupt;
those known as Assaji and Punabbasu, the residents of Kīṭāgiri, are shameless, evil monks.’"
They practice such improper conduct as this:
they plant flowering shrubs themselves or have them planted, they water them themselves or have them watered... [and so on] ...they practice various kinds of improper conduct.
Furthermore, Bhante, those people who were formerly faithful and confident have now become faithless and devoid of confidence.
"Those former sources of offerings for the Saṅgha have now been cut off;
virtuous bhikkhus are being neglected while wicked bhikkhus reside there.
It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would send bhikkhus to Kīṭāgiri so that this monastery at Kīṭāgiri may be restored."
“From there, Blessed One, I am coming.
Then, on this occasion and for this reason, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that those shameless and evil monks named Assaji and Punabbasuka, who reside at Kīṭāgiri, are practicing such improper conduct as this?”
They plant and cause to be planted *mālāvaccha* trees; they water and cause to be watered them... [and so on] ...they practice various kinds of improper conduct.
Those people, monks, who were formerly faithful and confident have now become faithless and lacking confidence;
those former gifts to the Saṅgha have also been cut off.
“Virtuous bhikkhus are being neglected while wicked bhikkhus dwell there?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them … [as before] …
"How indeed, monks, can those foolish men practice such improper conduct as this:

they will plant flowering shrubs themselves or have them planted; they will water them themselves or have them watered; they will pluck flowers themselves or have them plucked; they will string them themselves or have them strung;
they will make garlands with a single stalk themselves or have them made; they will make garlands with stalks on both sides themselves or have them made."
They will make flower clusters (*mañjarika*) and have them made; they will make *vidhūtika* ornaments and have them made; they will make ear-ornaments (*vaṭaṁsaka*) and have them made;
they will make garlands (*āveḷa*) and have them made; they will make breast-covers (*uracchada*) and have them made.
They [will give] single-stalked garlands to women of good family, daughters of good family, young maidens of good family, daughters-in-law of good family, and female slaves of good family.
They will wear garlands or have them worn; they will wear garlands with stalks on both ends or have them worn;
they will wear flower clusters or have them worn; they will wear loose flowers or have them worn; they will wear ear-ornaments or have them worn;
they will wear head-crests or have them worn; they will wear fillets or have them worn; they will wear breast-covers or have them worn.
They will eat from the same vessel as those women of good family, daughters of good family, young maidens of good family, daughters-in-law of good family, and female slaves of good family;
they will drink from the same water-pot; they will sit on the same seat; they will lie down on the same couch;
they will lie down on the same bedspread; they will lie down under the same coverlet; and they will lie down under the same bedspread and coverlet together.
They will eat at the wrong time; they will drink intoxicants; they will wear garlands, scents, and unguents;
they will dance, sing, play music, and cause others to dance;
and they will dance while [others] are dancing, sing while [others] are dancing, play music while [others] are dancing, and [cause others to dance] while [others] are dancing.

They will cause her to dance while she is singing; they will cause her to sing while she is dancing; they will cause her to sing while she is singing; they will cause her to sing while she is causing [others] to sing; they will cause her to cause [others] to sing while she is singing; they will cause her to cause [others] to sing while she is dancing; they will cause her to cause [others] to sing while she is singing.

They will cause her to dance while she is causing [others] to sing; they will cause her to sing while she is causing [others] to sing; they will cause her to cause [others] to sing while she is causing [others] to sing; they will cause her to cause [others] to sing while she is causing [others] to cause [others] to sing; they will cause her to cause [others] to cause [others] to sing while she is causing [others] to sing; they will cause her to cause [others] to cause [others] to sing while she is causing [others] to dance; they will cause her to cause [others] to cause [others] to sing while she is causing [others] to sing. They will cause her to dance while she is causing [others] to cause [others] to sing; they will cause her to sing while she is causing [others] to cause [others] to sing.
They will cause those who are languid to speak; they will cause those who are languid to exert themselves;
they will play at eight-row chess, they will play at ten-row chess;
they will play in the air, they will play on the path for circumambulation, they will play with dice, they will play with pebbles, and they will play with water-pots.
They will play with sticks in their hands; they will play with dice; they will play with cloth strips; they will play with crooked sticks; they will play with top-spinners;
they will play with whirling disks; they will play with leaf-plates; they will play with toy chariots; they will play with bows;
they will play with letter-games; and they will play with guessing-thoughts.
They will play; they will even play with dice.
They will train in elephant-riding, they will train in horsemanship, they will train in charioteering, they will train in archery, and they will train in swordsmanship.
They will run before elephants, they will run before horses, and they will both run and gallop before chariots.

They will shout out, they will clap their hands, they will wrestle, they will fight with their fists, and even spreading their outer robes in the middle of the arena, they will say to a dancer, “Dance here, sister,” and they will even give her a forehead kiss; they will practice various kinds of improper conduct.
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].
Having rebuked them and given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed Sāriputta and Moggallāna:
“Go, Sāriputtas, and having gone to Kīṭāgiri, perform an act of banishment from Kīṭāgiri against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka. They are your co-residents.
“Venerable sir, how shall we perform an act of banishment from Kīṭāgiri against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka? Those monks are fierce and harsh.”
“In that case, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, you should go together with many bhikkhus.
“Yes, Bhante,” Sāriputta and Moggallāna replied to the Blessed One.
“And furthermore, bhikkhus, it should be done in this way.”
First, the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka should be accused;
having been accused, they should be reminded; having been reminded, the offense should be laid against them.
Having laid the offense against them, a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
These monks Assaji and Punabbasuka are corrupters of families and of evil conduct. Their evil conduct is both seen and heard of; and families corrupted by them are both seen and heard of.

If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha carry out an act of banishment against the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka from Kīṭāgiri, [pronouncing]: ‘The monks Assaji and Punabbasuka must not dwell at Kīṭāgiri.’"
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
These monks Assaji and Punabbasuka are corrupters of families and of evil conduct. Their evil conduct is both seen and heard; and families corrupted by them are both seen and heard.
The Saṅgha performs an act of banishment from Kīṭāgiri against the monks Assaji and Puṇabbasuka, [decreeing]: “The monks Assaji and Puṇabbasuka must not reside at Kīṭāgiri.

Whoever among the venerable ones approves of performing this act of banishment from Kīṭāgiri against the monks Assaji and Puṇabbasuka—[to the effect that] “the monks Assaji and Puṇabbasuka must not reside at Kīṭāgiri”—let him remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I speak this matter...
A third time I speak this matter: Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs... let him speak.
The Saṅgha has performed the act of banishment from Kīṭāgiri against the monks Assaji and Punabbasu: "The monks Assaji and Punabbasu must not reside at Kīṭāgiri."
“It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.

Then the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, headed by Sāriputta and Moggallāna, went to Kīṭāgiri and performed an act of banishment against the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka from Kīṭāgiri: “The bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka [are to be expelled]...”
“You must reside at Kīṭāgiri.
Having been subjected by the Saṅgha to the formal act of banishment, they do not conduct themselves properly; they do not behave in accordance with the rules; they do not act toward a resolution;
they do not ask the bhikkhus for forgiveness; and they revile and abuse them, acting out of favoritism, ill will, and delusion.
They fall into states of fear; they depart, and they disrobe.
Those monks who have few desires... [as before] ...they grumble, complain, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka, having had a formal act of banishment carried out against them by the Saṅgha, not conduct themselves properly?"
“They will not let their hair fall, they will not act toward deliverance, they will not ask the monks for forgiveness;
they will revile and abuse them, and they will bring about being swayed by favoritism, being swayed by hatred, being swayed by delusion, and being swayed by fear;
they will even depart or disrobe.”
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha said:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhus Assaji and Punabbasuka, after the Sangha had performed an act of banishment against them, do not conduct themselves properly … and even go about disrobing?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One,
rebuked him … [as before] … And so, monks, you should recite this training rule thus: “If a monk, however,
living in dependence on a certain village or town, is a corrupter of families and of evil conduct;”
His evil conduct is both seen and heard of, and families corrupted by him are both seen and heard of.
That bhikkhu should be addressed by the bhikkhus thus:
"Venerable sir, you are a corrupter of families and one of evil conduct; your evil conduct is indeed seen and heard of."
Furthermore, families corrupted by the venerable one are both seen and heard of. Depart from this residence, venerable sir;
enough of your staying here.
If, when being addressed thus by the monks, that monk should say to those monks:

‘If monks who are swayed by favoritism, monks who are swayed by hatred, monks who are swayed by delusion, and monks who are swayed by fear, expel some for such an offense while not expelling others,’ that monk should be addressed by the monks as follows:
‘Venerable sir, do not speak thus. The monks are not swayed by favoritism; the monks are not swayed by hatred; the monks are not swayed by delusion; the monks are not swayed by fear.’
"Venerable sir, you are a corrupter of families and one of evil conduct.
Your evil conduct is both seen and heard of, and families corrupted by you are both seen and heard of. Depart from this residence;
enough of your staying here."
And if that bhikkhu, being thus addressed by the bhikkhus, should persist as before, that bhikkhu is to be pressed by the bhikkhus up to three times for the relinquishing of that [position].
If, being pressed up to three times, he relinquishes it, that is good;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.”
Now, a bhikkhu dwells depending on a certain village or town—
here, "village" includes the town, the city, and both the village and the town.
He dwells depending [on these].
Therein, robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick are dependent upon it.
As for "family," there are four families: the khattiya family, the brāhmaṇa family, the vessa family, and the sudda family.
A "corrupter of families" is one who corrupts families by means of flowers, fruits, powder, clay, tooth-sticks, bamboo, medicine, or running errands on foot.
A "one of evil conduct" is...

They plant flowering trees themselves or have them planted; they water them themselves or have them watered; they gather the flowers themselves or have them gathered; they string them themselves or have them strung.
They are both seen and heard:
those who are face-to-face see them, and those who are out of sight hear of them.
"And families are corrupted by him" means that having previously been faithful, they become faithless because of him; having been confident, they become lacking in confidence.
This is both seen and heard.
Those who are face-to-face see him; those who are behind hear him.
"That monk" refers to that monk who is a corrupter of families.
"By the bhikkhus" means by other bhikkhus. Those who see or hear [of it] should say to him:
"Venerable sir, you are a corrupter of families and one of evil conduct; indeed, the venerable one's evil conduct is both seen and heard."
Furthermore, families corrupted by the venerable one are both seen and heard of. Depart from this residence, venerable sir;
enough of your staying here.
If, when being addressed thus by the monks, that monk should say to those monks: “The monks are partial to their own desires...”
“Bhikkhus who follow hatred, bhikkhus who follow delusion, and bhikkhus who follow fear—
such are they that for an offense of this kind, they expel some and do not expel others.
He is a bhikkhu...
Regarding that monk who has been dealt with by the formal act:
"By the monks" means by other monks; those who see him or hear of him should speak to him thus:
“Do not speak thus, venerable sir. The monks do not act out of favoritism, nor do they act out of ill will, nor do they act out of delusion, nor do they act out of fear.
It is you, venerable sir, who are a corrupter of families and one of evil conduct. Your evil conduct is both seen and heard of;
families corrupted by you are both seen and heard of. Depart from this residence, venerable sir.”
“Enough of your staying here.
This should be said a second time,
and it should be said a third time.
If she relinquishes it, that is well.
If she does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If they hear [the accusation] and do not speak, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Then that monk, having been dragged into the midst of the Saṅgha, should be told:
"Venerable sir, do not speak thus. The monks do not act out of favoritism; the monks do not act out of ill will; the monks do not act out of delusion; the monks do not act out of fear.
It is you, venerable sir, who are a corrupter of families and of evil conduct. Indeed, the venerable one’s evil conduct is both seen and heard."
Furthermore, families corrupted by the venerable one are both seen and heard of. Depart from this residence, venerable sir;
enough of your staying here.
This should be said a second time as well.
A third time it should be said.
If he relinquishes it, that is well.
If he does not relinquish it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
That bhikkhu is to be formally admonished.
"And thus, bhikkhus, he is to be formally admonished:
A competent and capable bhikkhu should inform the Saṅgha:..."
‘Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs.
This bhikkhu named so-and-so, having been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of banishment, incites the bhikkhus to act out of favoritism, ill will, delusion, or fear.
He does not relinquish that matter.’
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha formally admonish the monk named so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
This is the motion.
Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me.
This monk named so-and-so, having been subjected by the Saṅgha to a formal act of banishment, incurs [the charge of] acting out of favoritism, ill will, delusion, or fear.
He does not relinquish that matter.
The Saṅgha exhorts the monk named so-and-so for the sake of his relinquishing that matter.
Whichever venerable one approves of the formal admonition of the monk named so-and-so for the sake of his relinquishing that matter, let him be silent; whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I speak this matter...
[as before] ...A third time I speak this matter... [as before].
“The Saṅgha has formally admonished the monk so-and-so for the relinquishing of that matter.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the motion.
With two proclamations, there are grave offenses (thullaccaya);
at the conclusion of the proclamation, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
For one who commits a saṅghādisesa offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the motion; with the two proclamations, the grave offenses are quelled.
*Saṅghādisesa*:
Only the Saṅgha grants probation for that offense, sends one back to the beginning, grants the *mānatta* penance, or rehabilitates one; neither a group nor a single individual does so.

Therefore it is called "an offense entailing suspension" (*saṅghādisesa*); it is the designation and synonym for that class of offenses. For this reason also, it is called "an offense entailing suspension."

If, regarding a legitimate legal procedure (*dhammakamma*), one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure and does not relinquish [the offense], there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
If, regarding a legitimate legal procedure, one is uncertain and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension.
If, regarding a legitimate legal procedure, one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure (*adhammakamma*) and does not relinquish it, there is an offense entailing suspension.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as a legitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one is uncertain of it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is an illegitimate legal procedure and one perceives it as an illegitimate legal procedure, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense for one who does not admonish,
or for one who relinquishes [the matter].
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The thirteenth training rule on corrupting families is concluded.
“Venerable sirs, the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules have been recited: nine that entail immediate offense upon commission, and four that become offenses after a third admonition.
Should a bhikkhu commit any one of these, for as long as he knowingly conceals it, for that same period must that bhikkhu undergo probation against his will.
Once the probation has been completed, the bhikkhu must further undertake the *bhikkhumānatta* penance for six nights.”
A monk who has completed the *mānatta* penance should be rehabilitated in a community of monks where there is a group of twenty monks.

If a community of monks that is short by even one from being twenty should rehabilitate that monk, that monk is not rehabilitated and those monks are to be censured; this is the proper procedure in such a case.
Therefore, I ask the Venerable Ones: "Are you pure in this matter?"
A second time I ask: “Are you pure in this matter? A third time I ask: “Are you pure in this matter?
The venerable ones are pure in this matter; therefore they are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The Thirteenfold [Section] is finished.
Its summary verse: Emission, bodily contact, [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates that the summary verse continues with further items not provided in the source fragment.*
Sexual misconduct and seeking one's own pleasure;
matchmaking, a hut, and a monastery, as well as groundless [accusations].
One who seeks only trifles, one who causes division, those who follow after such a person,
one who is difficult to speak to, and one who corrupts the family—
"Thirteen Saṅghādisesas.
The Section on Saṅghādisesa is finished.
